lessonPlan.title: Siddhartha unit
lessonPlan.author: Hermann Hesse
lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 9–12 (also 7–8; scales to graduate via rigor levels)
lessonPlan.schedule: 12 lessons of 90 minutes, 5 a week (block schedule), 3 weeks
essentialQuestions: What does Siddhartha suggest about the search for self-knowledge?
What does Siddhartha suggest about experience versus teaching?
What does Siddhartha suggest about the unity of all things?
What does Siddhartha suggest about the river and time?
What does Siddhartha suggest about love and attachment?
objectives: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly and implicitly.
Determine themes and analyze their development over the course of the novel.
Analyze how characters, setting and point of view interact.
Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in the text.
Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.
lessonPlan.differentiation: Every prompt and quiz has eleven rigor levels (Middle School through Graduate / PhD); the app applies student override, then class standard, then the automatic level.

activities: Daily 90-minute lesson: bell-ringer, vocabulary and etymology, background, I do / We do / You do, discussion, exit ticket, closure
Socratic seminar on the search for self-knowledge
Weekly writing prompt at assigned rigor
syllabus.assessment: Quiz average plus one graded writing prompt

wholeBookTest.title: Siddhartha: whole-book test

options: He is the son of a Brahmin

items.prompt: Where do they hear Gotama teach?
What does Siddhartha resolve to learn from?
Who ferries Siddhartha across the river?

options: As a game he does not take seriously
As a way to help the poor

items.prompt: What happens to Siddhartha over the years in the city?
What does Siddhartha intend to do at the river?
How does the son treat Siddhartha?
Who comes to the ferry at the end?

answerKey.answer: He is the son of a Brahmin
As a game he does not take seriously

shortAnswer: Explain how the search for self-knowledge develops from the beginning of the novel to the end. Use two chapters.
Explain how experience versus teaching develops from the beginning of the novel to the end. Use two chapters.
Explain how the unity of all things develops from the beginning of the novel to the end. Use two chapters.
wholeBookTest.essay: Choose one of the novel's central concerns (the search for self-knowledge, experience versus teaching, the unity of all things, the river and time, love and attachment) and argue how the ending reframes it.

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Write a five-paragraph essay explaining what Siddhartha teaches about the search for self-knowledge. Use at least three quotations from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Hermann Hesse develops the search for self-knowledge in Siddhartha. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Hermann Hesse develops the search for self-knowledge across Siddhartha. Trace the idea through at least three chapters and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of Siddhartha (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of the search for self-knowledge. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of the search for self-knowledge in Siddhartha. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: In a well-organized essay, analyze how Hermann Hesse uses a recurring literary element to shape the meaning of the search for self-knowledge in Siddhartha. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places Siddhartha's treatment of the search for self-knowledge in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on the search for self-knowledge in Siddhartha that reads the novel against its genre and period and engages two published critics.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on the search for self-knowledge in Siddhartha. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a capstone research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about the search for self-knowledge in Siddhartha, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on the search for self-knowledge in Siddhartha, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history.
